newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook - bearish, mogas still weak.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook - bearish, mogas still weak.

text.p: The outlook for European oil products prices looked glum again this week as mild weather tempers demand for gas oil, lengthy supply provided little comfort for gasoline, and fuel oil struggled to cope with poor Italian demand and good supply, traders said.
Industry events in London should stifle activity, too.
Gas oil premiums looked steady or weaker amid prospects of mild weather, dealers said. "Supplies are good and buyers are under no pressure with the weather," said one.
Good supply of heating oil should limit barge premiums to March IPE flat to +$2.
FOD Feb cargoes were seen around March IPE +$2-4.
German interest for DIN, which kept premiums up to +$6 last week, may wane.
Diesel should be helped by new buying into France to cover a refinery shutdown. Premiums should hold near March IPE +$18.
Gasoline was seen soft in northwest Europe due to a closed U.S. arbitrage and signs of growing supply for late February and early March.
"Maybe at the last week of February we'll start to see the pressure...At the moment every refiner is offering product into ARA," a trader at a major said.
Supply has not fully hit prices yet, he said, partly due to strength in naphtha and partly because in a contangoed market much of the product has been moved into storage.
The spread between prompt Eurograde and front-month Brent has held between $3.70 and $4 a barrel and could fall back to $3.50, traders said.
"We think the market is on its way down," a trader in Germany said.
Mediterranean prices should stay firm with no unsold cargoes left in February and demand bubbling up for low and mid-octane material from the Lebanon, Africa and South America.
Low octane material is also tight, pulled into the naphtha pool, he added.
Naphtha may be volatile and traders said recent strength, based on individual dealers' trading strategies rather than fundamental end user requirements, may remain in place.

But the spread between pipeline quality cargoes and cheaper, smaller parcels narrowed to $5 from $10 earlier last week, suggesting underlying negative fundamentals were limiting gains, he said. Small parcels from Russia and Europe were available.
The naphtha to crude crack spread, which blew out to $60-$70 a tonne last week, was expected to fall back toward $45-$50 .

Fuel oil was in the doldrums and unlikely to make more than half-hearted attempts at any gains. Latest data from Italy, showing a whopping 33 percent year-on-year fall in January's consumption by the power sector, underlined refiners' suspicion that Italian utility ENEL would continue to shun large quantities product from northwest Europe.

Supply from the Baltics was expected to top 800,000 tonnes in February, compared to 5-600,000 tonnes in January, and material fixed from sources across the Atlantic, loading in mid February, would further provide a damper to prices.
-- Nicholas Shaxson, London newsroom +44 171 542 8167
